objectives.text: analyse the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport
examine animal and plant cells
distinguish between asexual and sexual reproduction
examine various methods of asexual reproduction in plants
examine the process of sexual reproduction in plants
analyse growth patterns in plants
describe the methods used in the production of crops
relate soil fertility to the physical and chemical properties of soil
evaluate the impact of soil erosion on food production
outline various methods of asexual reproduction in animals
describe the structure and function of the sexual reproductive organs in humans
analyse the menstrual cycle in humans
discuss the stages of pregnancy
discuss the methods of birth control
assess the importance of pre-natal and post-natal care of mothers and babies
compare growth patterns of males and females
discuss the need for human population control
justify the need for transport systems within a living organism
relate the structures in transport systems to their functions
distinguish among the different blood groups
distinguish between excretion and egestion
explain the mechanism of excretion by the lungs, skin and kidneys in humans
identify the methods of excretion in flowering plants
describe the sense organs and their functions
relate the structures of the mammalian eye to their functions
analyse sight defects
relate the structures of the mammalian ear to their functions
relate the structures of the nervous system to their functions
relate the structures of the endocrine system to their functions
discuss selected microbes
discuss communicable/infectious disease
outline how the principles of immunisation are used in the control of communicable/infectious diseases
discuss non-communicable/infectious diseases
examine the physiological effects of exercise
evaluate the effects of drug use
discuss the importance of practising good personal hygiene
discuss conditions that encourage the breeding of household pests and parasites
recommend appropriate methods of pest control
describe various types of food contaminants
determine conditions which promote the growth of microorganisms
apply the principles used in food preservation

objective.text: analyse the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport

paper01.stem: The movement of water molecules from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution through a selectively permeable membrane is called
paper01.explanation: Osmosis is the movement of water molecules through a selectively permeable membrane from a dilute to a more concentrated solution.

objective.text: analyse the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport

paper01.stem: Which of the following processes requires energy from respiration?
paper01.explanation: Active transport moves particles against a concentration gradient and uses energy released in respiration.

objective.text: analyse the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport

paper01.stem: When a bottle of perfume is opened at the front of a classroom, students at the back soon smell it. This is because the perfume particles

options.A: are pumped by the air conditioner
options.B: move from a region of low concentration to one of high concentration
options.C: move from a region of high concentration to one of low concentration
options.D: pass through a selectively permeable membrane

paper01.explanation: The perfume spreads by diffusion, from where it is concentrated to where it is less concentrated.

objective.text: analyse the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport

paper01.stem: After the eruption of a volcano, ash was found in communities many kilometres away. The process which spreads the fine ash particles through the air is
paper01.explanation: Ash particles diffuse (spread) from where they are concentrated near the volcano to areas of lower concentration.

objective.text: analyse the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport

paper01.stem: Strips of fresh potato were placed in a concentrated salt solution for one hour. Which of the following observations would be expected?

options.A: The strips became longer and firmer.
options.B: The strips became shorter and soft.
options.C: The strips remained the same size.

paper01.explanation: Water leaves the potato cells by osmosis into the concentrated salt solution, so the cells lose turgor and the strips shrink and soften.

objective.text: analyse the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport

paper01.stem: The cell membrane is described as selectively permeable because it

options.A: allows only some substances to pass through
options.B: allows all substances to pass through
options.C: prevents all substances from passing through
options.D: is found only in plant cells

paper01.explanation: A selectively (partially) permeable membrane lets some molecules such as water through but holds back others.

objective.text: analyse the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport

paper01.stem: Root hair cells take in mineral salts from the soil even when the concentration of salts in the soil is lower than in the cell. This is possible by
paper01.explanation: Taking in ions against a concentration gradient needs energy: active transport.

objective.text: analyse the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport

paper01.stem: Diffusion is the movement of particles from a region of

options.A: low concentration to a region of high concentration
options.B: high concentration to a region of low concentration
options.C: high concentration to low concentration using energy
options.D: low concentration to high concentration through a membrane only

paper01.explanation: Diffusion is the net movement of particles down a concentration gradient; it needs no energy from the cell.

objective.text: analyse the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport

paper01.stem: Which of the following would INCREASE the rate of diffusion of a gas into a cell?
paper01.explanation: The greater the difference in concentration, the faster diffusion occurs.

objective.text: analyse the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport

paper01.stem: A red blood cell placed in distilled water swells and bursts because

options.A: salt enters the cell by diffusion
options.B: the cell membrane is fully permeable
options.D: water enters the cell by osmosis

paper01.explanation: Distilled water is more dilute than the cytoplasm, so water enters by osmosis. Animal cells have no cell wall to stop them bursting.

objective.text: analyse the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport

paper01.stem: A plant cell placed in pure water does NOT burst because

options.A: it has a strong cell wall

paper01.explanation: The cellulose cell wall resists the swelling cell and the cell becomes turgid.

objective.text: analyse the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport

paper01.stem: Cells in the lining of the small intestine absorb glucose even when the concentration of glucose in the gut is lower than in the cells. This is possible because the cells use
paper01.explanation: Uptake against a concentration gradient needs energy: active transport.

objective.text: analyse the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport

paper01.stem: Which of the following processes are involved in moving substances into and out of cells?
paper01.explanation: Cells use diffusion, osmosis and active transport.

objective.text: analyse the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport

paper01.stem: Smog from car exhaust spreads through a city on a still day MAINLY by
paper01.explanation: Gas particles move from where they are concentrated near the traffic to cleaner areas.

objective.text: analyse the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport

paper01.stem: Oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood because

options.C: the concentration of oxygen is higher in the alveoli than in the blood
options.D: the concentration of oxygen is lower in the alveoli

paper01.explanation: Oxygen moves down its concentration gradient.

objective.text: analyse the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport

paper01.stem: Dried raisins placed in water swell up because
paper01.explanation: The raisin cells are more concentrated than the water.

objective.text: analyse the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport

paper01.stem: What would be observed in the capillary tube after one hour?

options.D: The level of liquid does not change.

paper01.explanation: Water enters the sugar solution by osmosis through the membrane, so the liquid level rises in the capillary tube.

objective.text: analyse the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport

paper01.stem: Which process is demonstrated by this experiment?
paper01.explanation: Water moves from the distilled water (dilute) across a selectively permeable membrane into the sugar solution: osmosis.

objective.text: analyse the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport

paper01.stem: In which solution did the potato strips gain the MOST water?
paper01.explanation: The largest increase in length (12%) was in pure water, the most dilute solution.

objective.text: analyse the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport

paper01.stem: The concentration of the cell sap in the potato is MOST likely about
paper01.explanation: Where there is no change in length (about 0.4 mol dm⁻³) the solution has the same concentration as the cells.

objective.text: analyse the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport

paper01.stem: The strips in the 1.0 mol dm⁻³ solution became shorter because

options.A: sugar moved out of the cells
options.D: water moved out of the cells by osmosis

paper01.explanation: The solution was more concentrated than the cell sap, so the cells lost water.

objective.text: analyse the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport

paper01.stem: Which of the following conclusions can be drawn from this experiment?

options.A: Iodine molecules passed through the tubing but starch molecules did not.
options.B: Starch molecules passed out of the tubing.
options.C: Water could not pass through the tubing.
options.D: Both starch and iodine passed through the tubing.

paper01.explanation: Starch stayed inside (the water stayed brown) while iodine entered and stained the starch.

objective.text: analyse the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport

paper01.stem: The visking tubing in this experiment acts as a model of
paper01.explanation: Like a cell membrane, the tubing lets small molecules through but not large ones.

objective.text: examine animal and plant cells

paper01.stem: Which of the following structures are found in plant cells but NOT in animal cells?
paper01.explanation: Cell walls, chloroplasts and a large permanent vacuole are features of plant cells only.

objective.text: examine animal and plant cells

paper01.stem: Proteins are made in the cell by the
paper01.explanation: Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis.

objective.text: examine animal and plant cells

paper01.stem: Which cell structure contains chlorophyll?
paper01.explanation: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll which absorbs light for photosynthesis.

objective.text: examine animal and plant cells

paper01.stem: The jelly-like substance in which the chemical reactions of the cell take place is the
paper01.explanation: Most chemical reactions of the cell take place in the cytoplasm.

objective.text: examine animal and plant cells

paper01.stem: A cell was observed to have a nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane and many mitochondria, but no cell wall. The cell is MOST likely from
paper01.explanation: No cell wall means an animal cell; many mitochondria suggest an active cell such as muscle.

objective.text: examine animal and plant cells

paper01.stem: Root hair cells do NOT contain chloroplasts because

options.D: they are underground and receive no light

paper01.explanation: Chloroplasts would be of no use where there is no light for photosynthesis.

objective.text: examine animal and plant cells

paper01.stem: Which of the following is the function of the vacuole in a plant cell?

options.A: It stores cell sap and keeps the cell firm

paper01.explanation: The large permanent vacuole holds cell sap and helps keep the cell turgid.

objective.text: examine animal and plant cells

paper01.stem: The instrument used to observe cells from a prepared slide is the
paper01.explanation: Cells are too small to see without a microscope.

objective.text: examine animal and plant cells

paper01.stem: Which of the following is found in BOTH plant and animal cells?
paper01.explanation: Both types of cell respire aerobically and contain mitochondria.

objective.text: examine animal and plant cells

paper01.stem: A student observed cells from an onion bulb under a microscope. Which structure would she NOT see?
paper01.explanation: Onion bulb cells are underground storage cells with no chloroplasts.

objective.text: examine animal and plant cells

paper01.stem: Mitochondria are found in large numbers in
paper01.explanation: Active cells need lots of energy from respiration.

objective.text: examine animal and plant cells

paper01.stem: Which part of the cell controls the activities of the cell and contains the genetic information?
paper01.explanation: I labels the nucleus, which contains chromosomes (genetic information) and controls the cell.

objective.text: examine animal and plant cells

paper01.stem: In which structure is energy released during aerobic respiration?
paper01.explanation: IV labels a mitochondrion, the site of aerobic respiration.

objective.text: examine animal and plant cells

paper01.stem: The structure labelled III

options.B: gives the cell a fixed shape
options.C: controls what enters and leaves the cell

paper01.explanation: III is the cell membrane, which controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.

objective.text: examine animal and plant cells

paper01.stem: The structure labelled Q is the
paper01.explanation: Q points to one of the small oval bodies in the cytoplasm: a chloroplast.

objective.text: examine animal and plant cells

paper01.stem: Which labelled structure is made of cellulose and gives the plant cell a fixed shape?
paper01.explanation: P is the cell wall, made of cellulose.

objective.text: distinguish between asexual and sexual reproduction

paper01.stem: Which of the following is a feature of asexual reproduction?

options.B: Offspring are identical to the parent.
options.C: Gametes fuse to form a zygote.
options.D: There is great variety among the offspring.

paper01.explanation: Asexual reproduction involves one parent and mitosis, so the offspring are genetically identical (clones).

objective.text: distinguish between asexual and sexual reproduction

paper01.stem: The type of cell division which produces gametes is
paper01.explanation: Meiosis halves the chromosome number to produce gametes; mitosis produces identical body cells.

objective.text: distinguish between asexual and sexual reproduction

paper01.stem: A disadvantage of asexual reproduction in crops is that

options.C: a disease can wipe out the whole crop
options.D: good qualities of the parent are kept

paper01.explanation: All the offspring are identical, so a disease that attacks one plant can attack them all; there is no variation.

objective.text: distinguish between asexual and sexual reproduction

paper01.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of sexual reproduction?

options.B: Large numbers of offspring are produced quickly.
options.C: Offspring are exactly like the parent.
options.D: Offspring show variation and may adapt to change.

paper01.explanation: Fusion of gametes from two parents produces variation, which helps a species adapt to changing conditions.

objective.text: distinguish between asexual and sexual reproduction

paper01.stem: Sexual reproduction involves the fusion of

options.C: two nuclei from the same cell

paper01.explanation: Male and female gametes fuse at fertilisation to form a zygote.

objective.text: distinguish between asexual and sexual reproduction

paper01.stem: Mitosis produces cells which are

options.D: genetically identical to the parent cell

paper01.explanation: Mitosis is used for growth, repair and asexual reproduction.

objective.text: distinguish between asexual and sexual reproduction

paper01.stem: A farmer prefers to grow pineapples from suckers rather than from seeds because

options.C: the new plants have the same good qualities as the parent
options.D: seeds cannot grow in the Caribbean

paper01.explanation: Vegetative propagation produces offspring identical to the parent.

objective.text: distinguish between asexual and sexual reproduction

paper01.stem: Which of the following is a DISADVANTAGE of sexual reproduction?

options.A: Two parents are usually needed and it takes longer.
options.C: Offspring can adapt to new conditions.
options.D: Seeds can be dispersed far away.

paper01.explanation: Finding a mate or pollinator and forming seeds takes time and energy.

objective.text: distinguish between asexual and sexual reproduction

paper01.stem: Asexual reproduction involves the type of cell division called
paper01.explanation: Mitosis produces genetically identical cells.

objective.text: distinguish between asexual and sexual reproduction

paper01.stem: Which of the following statements is TRUE for sexual reproduction in plants?

options.A: Only one parent is ever involved.

paper01.explanation: Meiosis halves the chromosome number to form gametes.

objective.text: distinguish between asexual and sexual reproduction

paper01.stem: A disease-resistant variety of banana could be produced MOST easily by

options.A: taking cuttings from a diseased plant
options.C: tissue culture of a diseased plant

paper01.explanation: Variation from sexual reproduction provides new traits to select from.

objective.text: distinguish between asexual and sexual reproduction

paper01.stem: Which of the following is an ADVANTAGE of asexual reproduction to a farmer?

options.A: There is a lot of variation.
options.B: Plants can adapt quickly to new diseases.
options.D: Crops with the desired qualities are reproduced exactly.

paper01.explanation: Clones keep the qualities of the parent.

objective.text: examine various methods of asexual reproduction in plants

paper01.stem: Which of the following is an example of a corm?
paper01.explanation: Dasheen (eddoe) is a corm. Onion is a bulb, ginger is a rhizome and strawberry reproduces by runners.

objective.text: examine various methods of asexual reproduction in plants

paper01.stem: Ginger and canna lily reproduce by means of
paper01.explanation: Ginger grows from rhizomes, underground horizontal stems.

objective.text: examine various methods of asexual reproduction in plants

paper01.stem: A horizontal stem which grows along the surface of the soil and produces new plants at its nodes is called a
paper01.explanation: Runners (stolons), as in strawberry and some grasses, grow along the soil surface.

objective.text: examine various methods of asexual reproduction in plants

paper01.stem: Which method of artificial propagation involves joining the shoot of one plant onto the rooted stem of another plant?
paper01.explanation: In grafting a scion (shoot) is joined to a rootstock.

objective.text: examine various methods of asexual reproduction in plants

paper01.stem: A farmer wants to produce thousands of identical, disease-free banana plantlets from a few cells of one parent plant. Which method should he use?
paper01.explanation: Tissue culture grows many identical plantlets from small pieces of tissue under sterile conditions.

objective.text: examine various methods of asexual reproduction in plants

paper01.stem: Which of the following plants is COMMONLY propagated from stem cuttings?
paper01.explanation: Sugar cane is planted from stem cuttings (setts). Mango is usually grafted, onion grows from bulbs and dasheen from corms.

objective.text: examine various methods of asexual reproduction in plants

paper01.stem: An onion reproduces asexually by means of a
paper01.explanation: The onion bulb has fleshy leaves storing food around a short stem.

objective.text: examine various methods of asexual reproduction in plants

paper01.stem: Which of the following is an ARTIFICIAL method of vegetative propagation?
paper01.explanation: Budding is done by people; runners, corms and rhizomes are natural.

objective.text: examine various methods of asexual reproduction in plants

paper01.stem: Budding is often used to propagate citrus trees because it

options.D: combines a strong rootstock with a variety that produces good fruit

paper01.explanation: A bud of the desired variety is inserted into a hardy rootstock.

objective.text: examine various methods of asexual reproduction in plants

paper01.stem: Producing a genetically identical copy of an organism is called
paper01.explanation: Cloning produces genetically identical organisms; tissue culture is one method.

objective.text: examine various methods of asexual reproduction in plants

paper01.stem: Perennating organs such as corms and bulbs help plants to

options.D: survive unfavourable conditions such as a dry season

paper01.explanation: They store food so the plant can survive and regrow when conditions improve.

objective.text: examine the process of sexual reproduction in plants

paper01.stem: Which of the following is a feature of wind-pollinated flowers?

options.D: Feathery stigmas hanging outside the flower

paper01.explanation: Wind-pollinated flowers have feathery stigmas and anthers hanging outside, small dull petals and light, smooth pollen.

objective.text: examine the process of sexual reproduction in plants

paper01.stem: The transfer of pollen from the anther of one flower to the stigma of a flower on a DIFFERENT plant of the same kind is called
paper01.explanation: Cross-pollination is between different plants of the same species; it increases variation.

objective.text: examine the process of sexual reproduction in plants

paper01.stem: After fertilisation, the ovary of a flower develops into the
paper01.explanation: The ovary becomes the fruit and the ovules become the seeds.

objective.text: examine the process of sexual reproduction in plants

paper01.stem: Which of the following sequences represents the correct order of events in sexual reproduction in flowering plants?
paper01.explanation: Pollen must reach the stigma (pollination) before gametes fuse (fertilisation); seeds then form and later germinate.

objective.text: examine the process of sexual reproduction in plants

paper01.stem: The male part of a flower is the
paper01.explanation: The stamen is made up of the anther and filament.

objective.text: examine the process of sexual reproduction in plants

paper01.stem: The female part of a flower, made up of the stigma, style and ovary, is the
paper01.explanation: The carpel (pistil) is the female part.

objective.text: examine the process of sexual reproduction in plants

paper01.stem: The function of the sepals is to

options.C: protect the flower when it is a bud

paper01.explanation: Sepals enclose and protect the developing flower bud.

objective.text: examine the process of sexual reproduction in plants

paper01.stem: Cross-pollination is an advantage to a plant species because it
paper01.explanation: Genetic material from two plants combines, increasing variation.

objective.text: examine the process of sexual reproduction in plants

paper01.stem: Which of the following is a feature of insect-pollinated flowers?

options.B: Light, smooth pollen produced in large amounts

paper01.explanation: Scent, nectar and bright petals attract insects.

paper01.stem: After fertilisation, the ovule develops into the
paper01.explanation: The ovule becomes the seed; the ovary wall becomes the fruit.

objective.text: examine the process of sexual reproduction in plants

paper01.stem: Pollen grains are produced in the structure labelled
paper01.explanation: P is the anther, where pollen grains are made.

objective.text: examine the process of sexual reproduction in plants

paper01.stem: Which labelled structure develops into a seed after fertilisation?
paper01.explanation: T is an ovule; after fertilisation the ovule becomes the seed (the ovary becomes the fruit).

objective.text: examine the process of sexual reproduction in plants

paper01.stem: During pollination, pollen grains are transferred to the structure labelled
paper01.explanation: Q is the stigma, which receives pollen.

objective.text: examine the process of sexual reproduction in plants

paper01.stem: The structure labelled Q stores food for the embryo. Q is the
paper01.explanation: Cotyledons are the seed leaves that store food.

objective.text: analyse growth patterns in plants

paper01.stem: Which labelled structure grows into the first root of the seedling?
paper01.explanation: S is the radicle.

objective.text: analyse growth patterns in plants

paper01.stem: The structure labelled R develops into the
paper01.explanation: R is the plumule, the embryonic shoot.

objective.text: analyse growth patterns in plants

paper01.stem: Which of the following conditions is NOT needed for the germination of most seeds?
paper01.explanation: Germination needs water, oxygen and a suitable temperature. Light is not needed because the seedling uses stored food.

objective.text: analyse growth patterns in plants

paper01.stem: During germination of a bean seed, food for the growing seedling is obtained from the
paper01.explanation: The cotyledons store food which the embryo uses until the first leaves can photosynthesise.

objective.text: analyse growth patterns in plants

paper01.stem: Seeds soaked in water for a day germinate faster because water

options.B: provides all the food the seed needs
options.C: raises the temperature of the seed
options.D: softens the testa and activates the enzymes in the seed

paper01.explanation: Water softens the seed coat and allows enzymes to break down stored food.

objective.text: analyse growth patterns in plants

paper01.stem: Maize (corn) is an annual plant. This means it

options.B: flowers every year for ten years
options.C: completes its life cycle in one growing season

paper01.explanation: Annual plants such as corn and beans germinate, flower, set seed and die within a year.

objective.text: analyse growth patterns in plants

paper01.stem: Which of the following conditions affect the germination of seeds?
paper01.explanation: Water, oxygen and a suitable temperature are all needed.

objective.text: analyse growth patterns in plants

paper01.stem: In which test tube is germination MOST likely to take place?
paper01.explanation: Tube II has water, oxygen (air) and a suitable temperature - all three conditions needed for germination.

objective.text: analyse growth patterns in plants

paper01.stem: The seeds in test tube IV did NOT germinate because they lacked
paper01.explanation: Boiled water has had its dissolved oxygen removed and the oil layer stops air from dissolving back in.

objective.text: analyse growth patterns in plants

paper01.stem: The dry mass decreased during the first six days because

options.A: the seedlings absorbed too much water
options.D: stored food was used up in respiration before the leaves could photosynthesise

paper01.explanation: Until the first leaves open, the seedling respires its stored food, so dry mass falls.

objective.text: describe the methods used in the production of crops

paper01.stem: Growing plants with their roots in a nutrient solution instead of soil is called
paper01.explanation: Hydroponics grows plants in water containing dissolved mineral nutrients.

objective.text: describe the methods used in the production of crops

paper01.stem: A farmer grows corn in the first year, peas in the second year and sweet potato in the third year on the same plot. This practice is called
paper01.explanation: Crop rotation changes the crop grown on the same land each season; it helps restore nutrients and break pest cycles.

objective.text: describe the methods used in the production of crops

paper01.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of greenhouse farming?

options.D: Conditions such as temperature and humidity can be controlled.

paper01.explanation: A greenhouse protects crops and allows the farmer to control temperature, humidity and pests.

objective.text: describe the methods used in the production of crops

paper01.stem: Organic farming uses
paper01.explanation: Organic farming avoids synthetic chemicals and uses natural fertilisers such as compost and manure.

objective.text: describe the methods used in the production of crops

paper01.stem: Mrs Brown lives in an apartment with no yard. Which method would BEST allow her to grow her own herbs and vegetables?
paper01.explanation: Container gardening uses pots, buckets or boxes and is suited to small spaces.

objective.text: describe the methods used in the production of crops

paper01.stem: Growing different crops in alternate strips across a field is called
paper01.explanation: Strip planting (strip cropping) reduces erosion and pest spread.

objective.text: describe the methods used in the production of crops

paper01.stem: One advantage of hydroponics over growing crops in soil is that

options.B: crops can be grown in places with poor soil or little space

paper01.explanation: Plants get nutrients from solution, so soil quality does not matter.

objective.text: describe the methods used in the production of crops

paper01.stem: Crop rotation helps to control pests because

options.C: it attracts pests to the farm
options.D: pests that feed on one crop die out when a different crop is grown

paper01.explanation: Changing the crop breaks the life cycle of pests and diseases specific to one crop.

objective.text: describe the methods used in the production of crops

paper01.stem: Which of the following is a DISADVANTAGE of greenhouse farming?

options.A: Crops are protected from heavy rain
options.C: High cost of building and maintaining the greenhouse
options.D: Crops can be grown out of season

paper01.explanation: Greenhouses are expensive to set up and may need cooling in the tropics.

objective.text: describe the methods used in the production of crops

paper01.stem: An organic farmer wants to control aphids on her vegetables. Which method is she MOST likely to use?
paper01.explanation: Organic farming uses biological controls instead of synthetic chemicals.

objective.text: describe the methods used in the production of crops

paper01.stem: Tissue culture is used in crop production to

options.A: produce large numbers of disease-free identical plants quickly

paper01.explanation: Small pieces of tissue are grown on sterile nutrient jelly into many plantlets.

objective.text: relate soil fertility to the physical and chemical properties of soil

paper01.stem: Which of the following BEST describes loam soil?

options.A: A mixture of sand, clay and humus with good drainage and water retention
options.B: Large particles, drains very quickly, holds little water
options.C: Very small particles, drains poorly, easily waterlogged
options.D: Mainly stones with very little air

paper01.explanation: Loam is a mixture of sand, silt, clay and humus; it drains well yet holds enough water and air for plants.

objective.text: relate soil fertility to the physical and chemical properties of soil

paper01.stem: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria are found in the
paper01.explanation: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria live in root nodules of legumes such as peas and beans and convert nitrogen gas into nitrogen compounds.

objective.text: relate soil fertility to the physical and chemical properties of soil

paper01.stem: Which type of bacteria reduces soil fertility by converting nitrates in the soil to nitrogen gas?
paper01.explanation: Denitrifying bacteria change nitrates back to nitrogen gas, which is lost to the air.

objective.text: relate soil fertility to the physical and chemical properties of soil

paper01.stem: Humus improves soil fertility because it
statements: releases mineral nutrients as it decomposes
increases the water-holding capacity of the soil
paper01.explanation: Humus releases minerals as it decays, holds water like a sponge and binds particles into crumbs that improve aeration.

objective.text: relate soil fertility to the physical and chemical properties of soil

paper01.stem: Earthworms improve the fertility of soil by

options.B: increasing the acidity of the soil
options.C: making burrows which aerate and drain the soil

paper01.explanation: Earthworm burrows let air and water into the soil, and their casts mix in organic matter.

objective.text: relate soil fertility to the physical and chemical properties of soil

paper01.stem: A farmer found that the pH of his soil was 4.5. Which substance should he add to make the soil more suitable for most crops?
paper01.explanation: pH 4.5 is too acidic. Lime (calcium carbonate or calcium hydroxide) is a base that neutralises soil acidity.

objective.text: relate soil fertility to the physical and chemical properties of soil

paper01.stem: Compost is made mainly by the action of
paper01.explanation: Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down organic waste into compost.

objective.text: relate soil fertility to the physical and chemical properties of soil

paper01.stem: Which type of soil has the LARGEST particles?
paper01.explanation: Sand particles are the largest; clay particles are the smallest.

objective.text: relate soil fertility to the physical and chemical properties of soil

paper01.stem: Clay soil often becomes waterlogged because

options.B: its particles are very small and it drains poorly

paper01.explanation: Tiny particles leave very small pore spaces, so water drains slowly.

objective.text: relate soil fertility to the physical and chemical properties of soil

paper01.stem: A sedimentation test was carried out by shaking soil with water in a jar and leaving it to settle. Which layer would settle at the BOTTOM of the jar?
paper01.explanation: The largest, heaviest particles settle first; humus floats on top.

objective.text: relate soil fertility to the physical and chemical properties of soil

paper01.stem: Plants in waterlogged soil may die because

options.D: the roots do not get enough oxygen for respiration

paper01.explanation: Water fills the air spaces, so roots cannot respire aerobically.

objective.text: relate soil fertility to the physical and chemical properties of soil

paper01.stem: Nitrifying bacteria convert
paper01.explanation: Nitrifying bacteria oxidise ammonium compounds to nitrites and then nitrates, which plants absorb.

objective.text: relate soil fertility to the physical and chemical properties of soil

paper01.stem: Adding compost to sandy soil improves it by

options.A: increasing its ability to hold water and nutrients
options.D: reducing the number of soil organisms

paper01.explanation: Humus acts like a sponge and adds nutrients.

objective.text: relate soil fertility to the physical and chemical properties of soil

paper01.stem: Nematodes and earthworms are examples of
paper01.explanation: Many small organisms live in soil and affect its fertility.

objective.text: relate soil fertility to the physical and chemical properties of soil

paper01.stem: Which of the following soil pH values is BEST for growing most vegetable crops?
paper01.explanation: Most crops grow best in slightly acid to neutral soil (about pH 6-7).

objective.text: relate soil fertility to the physical and chemical properties of soil

paper01.stem: Which soil sample is MOST likely to be sandy soil?
paper01.explanation: P let the most water through; sandy soil has large particles and large air spaces, so it drains fastest.

objective.text: relate soil fertility to the physical and chemical properties of soil

paper01.stem: Which soil sample has the GREATEST water-holding capacity?
paper01.explanation: Q let the least water through, so it held the most water - typical of clay.

objective.text: relate soil fertility to the physical and chemical properties of soil

paper01.stem: Which layer contains the MOST humus and soil organisms?
paper01.explanation: W is the topsoil, where roots, humus and most soil organisms are found.

objective.text: evaluate the impact of soil erosion on food production

paper01.stem: Which of the following agricultural practices helps to REDUCE soil erosion on steep hillsides?
paper01.explanation: Terraces are flat steps cut into a hillside that slow down run-off.

objective.text: evaluate the impact of soil erosion on food production

paper01.stem: Rows of trees planted along the edge of a farm on a windy coast act as
paper01.explanation: Windbreaks reduce wind speed across the field and so reduce wind erosion.

objective.text: evaluate the impact of soil erosion on food production

paper01.stem: Which of the following is NOT a cause of soil erosion?
paper01.explanation: A cover crop protects the soil surface and roots bind the soil; the others expose or loosen the soil.

objective.text: evaluate the impact of soil erosion on food production

paper01.stem: Soil erosion reduces food production MAINLY because

options.B: more rain falls on the land

paper01.explanation: Erosion carries away the fertile topsoil which holds most of the nutrients and humus.

objective.text: evaluate the impact of soil erosion on food production

paper01.stem: Ploughing and planting across a slope instead of up and down the slope is known as
paper01.explanation: Contour farming follows the contour lines of the slope, forming ridges that slow run-off.

objective.text: evaluate the impact of soil erosion on food production

paper01.stem: Which of the following agents causes soil erosion on a bare, dry, flat field in the dry season?
paper01.explanation: Strong winds blow away dry, loose topsoil.

objective.text: evaluate the impact of soil erosion on food production

paper01.stem: Planting grass or a cover crop on bare land reduces soil erosion because the

options.A: roots bind the soil and the leaves protect it from raindrops
options.C: plants remove all the water from the soil

paper01.explanation: Vegetation shields the soil from rain impact and roots hold particles together.

objective.text: evaluate the impact of soil erosion on food production

paper01.stem: Which of the following is the MOST likely result of severe soil erosion in a farming community?

options.C: Lower crop yields and food shortages

paper01.explanation: Loss of fertile topsoil reduces the ability of the land to produce food.

objective.text: evaluate the impact of soil erosion on food production

paper01.stem: Bush fires increase the risk of soil erosion because they

options.B: remove the plant cover that protects the soil

paper01.explanation: Burnt land is left bare and exposed to wind and rain.

objective.text: evaluate the impact of soil erosion on food production

paper01.stem: Heavy rain on a hillside cleared of trees is MOST likely to cause
paper01.explanation: Without roots to bind soil, run-off washes it away.

objective.text: evaluate the impact of soil erosion on food production

paper01.stem: Which of the following farming methods reduces soil erosion by wind?
paper01.explanation: Trees reduce wind speed across fields.

objective.text: evaluate the impact of soil erosion on food production

paper01.stem: Rivers near farms which suffer from soil erosion often become muddy. This can
paper01.explanation: Sediment smothers reefs and fills channels.

objective.text: outline various methods of asexual reproduction in animals

paper01.stem: Amoeba reproduces by splitting into two identical cells. This method of reproduction is
paper01.explanation: Binary fission: one cell divides into two identical daughter cells.

objective.text: outline various methods of asexual reproduction in animals

paper01.stem: Hydra reproduces asexually when a small outgrowth develops on its body and later breaks away. This process is called
paper01.explanation: In budding a new individual grows as an outgrowth of the parent.

objective.text: outline various methods of asexual reproduction in animals

paper01.stem: The development of an egg into a new individual WITHOUT fertilisation is called
paper01.explanation: Parthenogenesis occurs in organisms such as aphids and drone honeybees.

objective.text: outline various methods of asexual reproduction in animals

paper01.stem: A starfish that loses an arm can grow a new starfish from the broken arm. This is an example of
paper01.explanation: Fragmentation: a new organism grows from a piece of the parent.

objective.text: outline various methods of asexual reproduction in animals

paper01.stem: Which of the following statements about asexual reproduction in animals is TRUE?

options.C: Only one parent is involved and offspring are identical to it.

paper01.explanation: Asexual reproduction involves one parent and no fusion of gametes.

objective.text: outline various methods of asexual reproduction in animals

paper01.stem: Bacteria and Paramecium MOST commonly reproduce by
paper01.explanation: They split into two identical cells.

objective.text: outline various methods of asexual reproduction in animals

paper01.stem: Male honeybees (drones) develop from unfertilised eggs. This is an example of
paper01.explanation: Parthenogenesis: development from an unfertilised egg.

objective.text: outline various methods of asexual reproduction in animals

paper01.stem: Which of the following organisms can reproduce by fragmentation?
paper01.explanation: A cut flatworm can regrow into two organisms.

objective.text: outline various methods of asexual reproduction in animals

paper01.stem: A disadvantage of asexual reproduction in animals is that
paper01.explanation: Identical offspring may all be affected by the same change.

objective.text: outline various methods of asexual reproduction in animals

paper01.stem: Yeast cells reproduce asexually by
paper01.explanation: A small bud grows from the parent cell.

objective.text: describe the structure and function of the sexual reproductive organs in humans

paper01.stem: The ring of muscle at the neck of the uterus which dilates during birth is the
paper01.explanation: The cervix dilates (widens) during the first stage of labour.

objective.text: describe the structure and function of the sexual reproductive organs in humans

paper01.stem: Sperm are produced in the
paper01.explanation: Sperm are made in the testes; the epididymis stores them.

objective.text: describe the structure and function of the sexual reproductive organs in humans

paper01.stem: Which of the following structures carries sperm from the epididymis towards the urethra?
paper01.explanation: The sperm duct (vas deferens) carries sperm from the epididymis to the urethra.

objective.text: describe the structure and function of the sexual reproductive organs in humans

paper01.stem: The testes are held in the scrotum outside the body because

options.A: they are too large to fit inside the abdomen
options.B: sperm production needs a temperature slightly lower than body temperature
options.C: sperm need to be exposed to light

paper01.explanation: Sperm develop best at about 2-3 °C below core body temperature.

objective.text: describe the structure and function of the sexual reproductive organs in humans

paper01.stem: The prostate gland and seminal vesicles

options.A: produce fluid in which sperm swim

paper01.explanation: They add fluid containing nutrients to the sperm to form semen.

objective.text: describe the structure and function of the sexual reproductive organs in humans

paper01.stem: The epididymis
paper01.explanation: Sperm mature and are stored in the coiled epididymis.

objective.text: describe the structure and function of the sexual reproductive organs in humans

paper01.stem: In the male, the tube which carries both urine and semen out of the body is the
paper01.explanation: The urethra passes through the penis.

objective.text: describe the structure and function of the sexual reproductive organs in humans

paper01.stem: Cowper's glands
paper01.explanation: Cowper's glands add a small amount of fluid that lubricates and neutralises the urethra.

objective.text: describe the structure and function of the sexual reproductive organs in humans

paper01.stem: Which of the following correctly matches a female organ with its function?

options.A: Oviduct - carries the ovum to the uterus

paper01.explanation: The oviduct carries the egg from the ovary to the uterus; fertilisation also occurs there.

objective.text: describe the structure and function of the sexual reproductive organs in humans

paper01.stem: A woman whose oviducts are blocked is unlikely to become pregnant because
paper01.explanation: The oviduct is where sperm meets the egg.

objective.text: describe the structure and function of the sexual reproductive organs in humans

paper01.stem: Testosterone is produced by the
paper01.explanation: The testes produce sperm and testosterone.

objective.text: describe the structure and function of the sexual reproductive organs in humans

paper01.stem: Fertilisation normally takes place in the structure labelled
paper01.explanation: Q is the oviduct (Fallopian tube), where sperm normally meets the egg.

points: Produces pollen grains (male gametes).

Large, brightly coloured petals attract insects (1)
Scent attracts insects (1)

Suitable scale using at least 75% of the grid
Smooth curve drawn through all points

markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: State the THREE conditions necessary for the germination of the bean seeds.

points: Water
Oxygen
Suitable (warm) temperature

points: Cell wall present
Chloroplasts present
Large (permanent) vacuole
Regular/fixed shape

parts.label: (b)
parts.context: Mrs Clarke sells lettuce at an open market. By midday the leaves wilt, but after she sprinkles them with water they become firm again.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Define the term 'osmosis'.

points: The movement of water molecules from a dilute solution (high water concentration) to a more concentrated solution (low water concentration) through a selectively permeable membrane.

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain how sprinkling water on the lettuce causes the leaves to become firm again.

points: The water outside is more dilute than the cell sap (1)
water enters the cells by osmosis through the selectively permeable membrane (1)
the vacuoles swell and press against the cell wall, making the cells turgid/firm (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

parts.context: The heart pumps blood around the body.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Name the blood vessel which carries blood from the heart to the lungs.

points: Pulmonary artery

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: The wall of the left ventricle is much thicker than that of the right ventricle. Explain why.

points: The left ventricle pumps blood to all parts of the body (1)
so it must produce a higher pressure/more force than the right ventricle, which pumps only to the lungs (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: State the function of the valves in the heart.

points: To prevent the backflow of blood / keep blood flowing in one direction.

items.label: (iv)
items.prompt: Name the type of blood cell which transports oxygen.

points: Red blood cell (erythrocyte)

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Complete Table 2 by calculating the volume of water RETAINED by EACH soil sample.

points: P: 30 cm³
Q: 75 cm³
R: 52 cm³

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Identify which sample, P, Q or R, is MOST likely to be clay. Give a reason for your answer.

points: It retained the most water/drained the least because clay has very small particles and small air spaces (1)
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for identification; 1 mark for reason

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: State ONE variable which the students MUST keep constant in this experiment.

points: Mass/volume of soil
Volume of water added
Time allowed for drainage
Size of funnel/filter paper

parts.label: (b)
parts.context: One student claimed that soil taken from under trees contains more humus than soil taken from an open field.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State a suitable hypothesis to test the student's claim.

points: Soil from under trees contains more humus (organic matter) than soil from an open field.
OR: If soil from under trees is heated, it will lose more mass than an equal mass of soil from an open field.
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for a clearly stated hypothesis; 1 mark for a testable hypothesis

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Outline a suitable method the student could use to test the hypothesis in (b) (i).

points: Dry equal masses of the two soil samples (e.g. in an oven at about 100 °C) and weigh each (1)
Heat each sample strongly in a crucible to burn off the humus (1)
Cool and reweigh; repeat heating until the mass is constant (1)
Calculate the loss in mass for each sample and compare - the greater loss shows more humus (1)
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark each for any four logical steps

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Explain how humus improves the fertility of soil.

points: Humus decomposes and releases mineral nutrients (1)
it increases the water-holding capacity of the soil (1)
it binds particles into crumbs, improving aeration/drainage/soil structure (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

parts.label: (c)
parts.context: Many farms in the Caribbean are on steep hillsides.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State TWO causes of soil erosion on hillsides.

points: Heavy rainfall/run-off
Deforestation/removal of vegetation
Bush fires
Ploughing up and down the slope
Overgrazing

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Describe how terracing helps to reduce soil erosion.

points: Terraces are flat steps cut into the slope (1)
which slow down the flow of run-off water so that less soil is carried away (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Explain why soil erosion reduces food production.

points: The fertile topsoil containing nutrients/humus is removed, so crops grow poorly / less land is available for farming.

paper02.title: The menstrual cycle, birth control and pre-natal care

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: Figure 4 shows changes in the thickness of the lining of the uterus of a woman over a 28-day menstrual cycle.
parts.figure: Figure 4. Thickness of the uterine lining during a menstrual cycle

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Using Figure 4, state the days on which menstruation occurs.

points: Days 0/1 to 5

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Define the term 'ovulation' and state on which day it is MOST likely to occur in this cycle.

points: Ovulation is the release of an ovum (egg) from the ovary (1)

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Explain the role of the hormone progesterone in the menstrual cycle.

points: Progesterone is produced after ovulation (by the corpus luteum) (1)
it keeps the uterine lining thick/maintains it ready for implantation; when progesterone falls, the lining breaks down (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

parts.label: (b)
parts.context: A young couple wishes to plan their family.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Complete Table 3 by giving ONE example of EACH method of birth control.

points: Barrier: condom / diaphragm / cervical cap / IUD
Hormonal: pill / injection / patch / implant
Surgical: vasectomy / tubal ligation

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State ONE advantage and ONE disadvantage of the condom as a method of birth control.

points: Advantage: protects against STIs / cheap / easily available / no side effects
Disadvantage: may tear or slip off / must be used every time / may reduce sensation

parts.label: (c)
parts.context: Pre-natal care is important for the health of mother and baby.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State TWO practices which a pregnant woman should follow to ensure a healthy baby.

points: Eat a balanced diet (with iron/folic acid)
Avoid smoking, alcohol and drugs
Attend regular pre-natal clinic visits
Avoid X-rays
Get suitable exercise and rest

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain why breastfeeding is recommended for newborn babies.

points: Breast milk contains antibodies which give the baby passive immunity (1)
it has the correct balance of nutrients and is easily digested (1)
it is clean/sterile, at the right temperature and free, and helps bonding (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

paper02.title: Surface area to volume ratio and transpiration

parts.context: Students cut three cubes of agar jelly containing a pink indicator. They placed the cubes in dilute acid, which turns the indicator colourless, and timed how long it took for each cube to become completely colourless. Their results are shown in Table 4.

items.prompt: Complete Table 4 by calculating the surface area of the 3 cm cube and the surface area to volume ratio of the 2 cm cube.

points: Surface area of 3 cm cube = 6 × 3 × 3 = 54 cm² (1)
Ratio for 2 cm cube = 24 : 8 = 3 : 1 (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Describe the relationship between the surface area to volume ratio and the time taken for the acid to reach the centre of the cube.

points: As the surface area to volume ratio decreases (1)
the time taken for the acid to diffuse to the centre increases (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Use the results of the experiment to explain why large organisms such as humans need a transport system.

points: Large organisms have a small surface area to volume ratio (1)
diffusion alone would be too slow to supply substances to cells deep inside the body (1)
so a transport system (blood/circulatory system) is needed to carry oxygen and nutrients to all cells and remove wastes (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State a suitable hypothesis for this investigation.

points: The rate of transpiration increases when the shoot is exposed to wind.
OR: The air bubble will move a greater distance in a fixed time when the fan is switched on.
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for a clearly stated hypothesis; 1 mark for a testable hypothesis

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State the manipulated variable and the responding variable in this investigation.

points: Manipulated: presence/absence (or speed) of wind from the fan (1)
Responding: distance moved by the air bubble in a fixed time / rate of water uptake (1)

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: State ONE precaution the student should take to obtain reliable results.

points: Cut the shoot under water to prevent air entering the xylem
Make sure the apparatus is airtight (seal joints with Vaseline)
Keep light and temperature the same
Repeat readings and find an average

items.label: (iv)
items.prompt: Predict how the movement of the air bubble would change if the leafy shoot were covered with a clear plastic bag. Explain your answer.

points: The bubble would move more slowly (1)
because the air inside the bag becomes humid, reducing the concentration gradient of water vapour, so less water evaporates from the leaves (1)
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for prediction; 1 mark for explanation

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Name the tissue in the stem which carries water from the roots to the leaves.

points: Xylem

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State TWO environmental factors, other than wind, which affect the rate of transpiration.

points: Temperature
Humidity
Light intensity

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Explain why transpiration is important to a plant.

points: It creates a pull which draws water up the xylem from the roots (1)
it carries dissolved mineral salts to the leaves (1)
evaporation cools the leaves (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Identify the parts labelled P, Q and R.

points: P - glomerulus/Bowman's capsule
Q - first (proximal) coiled tubule
R - loop of Henle

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Describe how urine is formed in the nephron.

points: Blood is filtered under high pressure in the glomerulus/Bowman's capsule (ultrafiltration) (1)
useful substances such as glucose, some salts and water are reabsorbed into the blood in the tubule (selective reabsorption) (1)
the remaining urea, excess water and salts pass down the collecting duct as urine (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

parts.label: (b)
parts.context: Andre drank two litres of water on a cool morning. Later that day he played football in the hot sun and drank very little.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Define the term 'excretion'.

points: The removal of waste products of metabolism from the body.

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain how antidiuretic hormone (ADH) would affect the volume of urine Andre produced while playing football in the hot sun.

points: He loses water by sweating so the blood becomes more concentrated (1)
the pituitary gland releases more ADH (1)
the collecting ducts reabsorb more water, so a small volume of concentrated urine is produced (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Distinguish between 'excretion' and 'egestion'.

points: Excretion is the removal of metabolic wastes made by body cells, e.g. urea, CO₂ (1)
egestion is the removal of undigested food (faeces) which was never part of the body cells (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Name ONE waste product excreted by the lungs and ONE excreted by the skin.

points: Lungs: carbon dioxide / water vapour (1)
Skin: water / salts / (small amount of) urea (1)

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: State ONE reason why a patient may need dialysis.

points: The kidneys have failed/stopped working and cannot remove urea and excess water/salts from the blood.

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: Kerry-Ann measured her pulse rate at rest, then ran on the spot for 4 minutes and measured her pulse rate every minute after she stopped. Her results are shown in Table 5.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: On the grid provided, plot a graph of pulse rate against time after exercise. You MUST label EACH axis and join the points with a smooth curve.

points: Axes labelled with units
Suitable scale
Smooth curve
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for correct plotting of points (all points = 2; at least half = 1); 1 mark for both axes labelled with units; 1 mark for an appropriate scale (at least 75% of the grid used); 1 mark for a smooth line/curve joining the points

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Kerry-Ann's resting pulse rate was 72 beats per minute. Using your graph, state how long it took for her pulse to return to the resting rate.

points: 6 minutes

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Explain why the pulse rate was high immediately after exercise.

points: During exercise the muscles respire faster and need more oxygen and glucose (1)
the heart beats faster to deliver more blood carrying oxygen and glucose to the muscles (1)
and to remove the extra carbon dioxide / repay the oxygen debt (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

parts.label: (b)
parts.context: Kerry-Ann's teacher suggests that students who exercise regularly have a lower resting pulse rate than students who do not exercise.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State a suitable aim for an investigation to test the teacher's suggestion.

points: To find out whether students who exercise regularly have a lower resting pulse rate than students who do not exercise.
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for aim related to the suggestion

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State TWO variables that should be controlled in this investigation.

points: Age of students
Gender
Time of day/length of rest before measuring
Method of taking the pulse/duration of counting
Health of students (no illness)

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: State TWO long-term effects of regular exercise on the body.

points: Stronger heart muscle / lower resting heart rate
Improved muscle tone
Increased lung capacity
Reduced body fat / helps balance energy input and output
Lower risk of hypertension/diabetes

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Name TWO non-communicable diseases whose risk is reduced by regular exercise.

points: Diabetes (Type 2)
Hypertension
Heart disease
Obesity
Stroke

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain how a diet high in salt may lead to hypertension.

points: Excess salt causes the body to retain water, increasing blood volume (1)
which raises the pressure of blood on the artery walls (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: State ONE effect of uncontrolled hypertension on the body.

points: Stroke
Heart attack/heart failure
Kidney damage
Damage to blood vessels/eyes
markScheme.guidance: Any one effect, correctly stated with detail, 2 marks; effect only, 1 mark

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Identify the parts labelled A, C and E.

points: A - cornea
C - lens
E - retina

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Describe how the eye adjusts to focus on a NEAR object.

points: The ciliary muscles contract (1)
the suspensory ligaments slacken/become loose (1)
the lens becomes fatter/more convex so light is bent more and focused on the retina (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

parts.label: (b)
parts.context: Tamika cannot read the writing on the classroom board, but she can read her textbook clearly.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Name Tamika's sight defect.

points: Short sight / myopia

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain how the defect named in (b) (i) can be corrected.

points: Light from distant objects is focused in front of the retina (1)
a concave (diverging) lens is placed in front of the eye (1)
which spreads out the light rays so that they focus on the retina (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State the function of the cochlea.

points: Converts sound vibrations into nerve impulses (for hearing).

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain why a person's ears may 'pop' when an aeroplane is taking off.

points: The air pressure outside falls, so pressure on the two sides of the ear drum becomes unequal (1)

points: A vaccine contains dead/weakened pathogens or parts of them (antigens) (1)

if the real pathogen enters later, antibodies are produced quickly and destroy it before the person becomes ill (1)

items.prompt: Complete Table 1 by calculating the change in length of the strips in the 0.2 and 0.6 mol dm⁻³ solutions.

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: On the grid provided, plot a graph of change in length against concentration of sugar solution.

points: Points (0,+6) (0.2,+3) (0.4,0) (0.6,-3) (0.8,-5) plotted with a y-axis that includes negative values
Axes labelled with units
Suitable scale
Smooth line/curve
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for correct plotting of points (all points = 2; at least half = 1); 1 mark for both axes labelled with units; 1 mark for an appropriate scale (at least 75% of the grid used); 1 mark for a smooth line/curve joining the points

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Explain why the strip in the 0.0 mol dm⁻³ solution became longer.

points: Pure water is more dilute than the cell sap of the potato (1)
so water entered the cells by osmosis through the selectively permeable membranes (1)
the cells swelled/became turgid, so the strip got longer (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (iv)
items.prompt: Use your graph to estimate the concentration of the cell sap in the potato. Give a reason for your answer.

points: About 0.4 mol dm⁻³ (1)

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State TWO variables Keisha should have kept constant.

points: Initial length/size of strips
Volume of solution
Time in the solution
Type/source of potato
Temperature

items.prompt: Suggest ONE way Keisha could make her results more reliable.

points: Use several strips for each concentration and find the average / repeat the experiment.

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Distinguish between osmosis and active transport.

points: Osmosis is the passive movement of water from a dilute to a concentrated solution across a selectively permeable membrane (1)

items.prompt: Explain why fish can be preserved by salting.

the join is tied and sealed with tape/wax until it grows together (1)

items.label: (iii)

points: Large numbers of plantlets produced quickly
Plants are disease-free
Plants are identical with the desired qualities
Can be done all year in a small space

Tuber - sweet potato/Irish potato

paper02.title: Hand washing and the growth of bacteria

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: A class investigated how well different methods of hand washing remove bacteria. Each student pressed a fingertip on sterile nutrient agar in a petri dish after washing. The dishes were sealed and kept at 30 °C for two days, and then the colonies of bacteria were counted. The results are shown in Table 3.

table.title: TABLE 3: BACTERIAL COLONIES AFTER HAND WASHING

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: On the grid provided, draw a bar chart to show the results in Table 3.

points: Four bars of correct heights
Axes labelled (Method of hand washing; Number of colonies)
Bars of equal width and equally spaced
Suitable scale

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Calculate the percentage decrease in colonies when hands were washed with soap and water compared with no washing. Show your working.

markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for working; 1 mark for answer

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: State a conclusion from these results.

points: Washing with soap and water removes the most bacteria from the hands.

items.label: (iv)
items.prompt: Explain why the dishes were kept at 30 °C.

points: 30 °C is a warm/optimal temperature for bacterial growth (1)
so the colonies grow large enough to be counted in two days (1) (a temperature below 37 °C reduces the chance of growing human pathogens)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (v)
items.prompt: State TWO safety precautions the students should take in this experiment.

points: Keep dishes sealed/taped and do not open them after incubation
Wash hands after handling the dishes
Sterilise/dispose of dishes safely (autoclave/bleach)
Do not incubate at 37 °C

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Name ONE control that should have been included in the investigation and state its purpose.

points: A dish of sterile agar not touched (1) to show that the agar itself was not contaminated (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain why practising good personal hygiene is important for a food handler.

points: Hands and body may carry pathogens such as bacteria from the toilet or skin (1)
these can contaminate food and multiply (1)
causing food poisoning/spread of disease to customers (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State TWO conditions which promote the growth of microorganisms in food.

points: Moisture
Warm/optimum temperature
Nutrients
Suitable pH

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Give ONE example of a useful effect of microorganisms in food production.

points: Yeast (1) makes bread rise / produces alcohol in wine and beer (1)
Bacteria (1) turn milk into yoghurt or cheese (1)

points: The distance decreased with each attempt / reaction time got shorter (1)

Effector: muscles of the hand/fingers (1)

parts.figure: Figure 2. A foetus in the uterus

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Identify the structures labelled P, Q and S.

points: P - placenta
Q - umbilical cord
S - cervix (vagina)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State TWO substances which pass from the mother to the foetus and ONE which passes from the foetus to the mother.

points: Mother to foetus: oxygen, glucose, amino acids, antibodies, water, minerals (any two) (2)
Foetus to mother: carbon dioxide / urea (1)

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Explain why a pregnant woman who smokes may give birth to a baby with a low birth weight.

points: Carbon monoxide in smoke combines with haemoglobin (1)
so less oxygen reaches the foetus through the placenta (1)
the foetus respires and grows less, so it is smaller at birth (nicotine also narrows blood vessels) (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Describe what happens during the three stages of labour.

points: Stage 1: the uterus contracts and the cervix dilates (1)
Stage 2: strong contractions push the baby out head first (crowning and expulsion) (1)
Stage 3: the placenta separates and is expelled as the afterbirth (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State ONE use of ultrasound during pregnancy.

points: Check the growth/position of the foetus
Detect twins
Detect abnormalities
Estimate the due date

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Explain why babies are immunised against diseases such as polio.

points: The vaccine stimulates the baby to make antibodies and memory cells (1)
so the baby is protected if it later meets the disease (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: Samples of fresh milk were kept at 4 °C and at 30 °C. The pH of each sample was measured every 12 hours. The results are shown in Table 2.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: On the grid provided, plot graphs of pH against time for BOTH samples on the same axes. Include a key.

points: Both sets of points correctly plotted (2)
Key (1)
Axes labelled with units (1)
Suitable scale (1)
Lines/curves drawn neatly (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Describe how the pH of the milk kept at 30 °C changed over 48 hours.

points: It decreased from 6.7 to 4.5 - the milk became more acidic.

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Explain why the pH of the milk at 30 °C fell.

points: Bacteria in the milk multiplied rapidly at the warm temperature (1)
they fed on the milk sugar (lactose) (1)
producing lactic acid, which lowered the pH (the milk soured) (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (iv)
items.prompt: Explain why the pH of the milk at 4 °C hardly changed.

points: Low temperature slows down the growth/activity of bacteria (1)
so very little acid was produced (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Pasteurisation involves heating milk to about 72 °C for 15 seconds and cooling it quickly. Explain how this helps milk to stay fresh longer.

points: Heating kills most of the bacteria in the milk (1)
rapid cooling and refrigeration stop the remaining bacteria from multiplying (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State TWO conditions, other than temperature, which microorganisms need to grow.

points: Moisture
Nutrients/food
Suitable pH
Oxygen (for some)

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Name ONE food made using bacteria and milk.

points: Yoghurt / cheese

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State TWO precautions to take when handling the milk samples in this experiment.

points: Do not taste the milk
Keep containers covered
Use a clean pH probe/rinse between readings
Wash hands after handling
Label samples clearly

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Distinguish between a pathogen and a vector.

points: A pathogen causes disease; a vector carries the pathogen from one host to another.

parts.figure: Figure 3. Section through a kidney

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Identify the parts labelled P, R and S.

points: P - cortex
R - pelvis
S - ureter

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State the main function of the kidneys in excretion.

points: To remove urea, excess water and excess salts from the blood (forming urine).

parts.label: (b)
parts.context: Table 3 shows the concentration of some substances in the blood plasma entering a kidney and in the urine of a healthy person.

table.title: TABLE 3: COMPOSITION OF PLASMA AND URINE

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Explain why there is no protein in the urine.

points: Protein molecules are too large (1)
to pass through the walls of the glomerulus during ultrafiltration (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain why there is glucose in the plasma but none in the urine.

points: Glucose is filtered out of the blood in the glomerulus (1)
but all of it is reabsorbed back into the blood in the tubule (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Suggest why the concentration of urea is much higher in urine than in plasma.

points: Most of the water filtered is reabsorbed (1)
while urea is not reabsorbed, so it becomes concentrated in the urine (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Name the hormone which controls the water content of the blood, and the gland which releases it.

points: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) (1)
Pituitary gland (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State TWO ways in which the skin helps to control body temperature when the body is too hot.

points: Sweat glands produce more sweat which evaporates
Blood vessels near the surface dilate so more heat is lost
Hairs lie flat

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: State ONE disadvantage of dialysis for a patient with kidney failure.

points: Time-consuming - several hours, several times a week
Expensive
Restricted diet and fluid intake
Risk of infection

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: Students shook 100 cm³ of soil from each of two gardens with water in measuring cylinders and left them to settle. They measured the height of each layer. The results are shown in Table 4.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: On the grid provided, draw a bar chart to compare the composition of the two soils. Use a key.

points: Bars for both gardens for each layer, correct heights (2)
Key to distinguish X and Y (1)
Axes labelled (1)
Suitable scale and equal bar widths (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain why gravel and sand settle at the bottom while humus floats.

points: Gravel and sand particles are large and heavy/dense, so they settle first (1)
humus is organic matter with a low density, so it floats (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Identify the type of soil in EACH garden.

points: Garden X - sandy soil (1)
Garden Y - clay soil (1)

parts.label: (b)
parts.context: The owner of garden Y finds that water collects on the surface after rain and his vegetables grow poorly.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Explain why the vegetables grow poorly in garden Y.

points: Clay has very small particles and pore spaces, so it drains poorly and becomes waterlogged (1)
the air spaces fill with water, so roots lack oxygen (1)
and cannot respire to absorb minerals, so growth is poor (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Suggest TWO ways to improve the soil in garden Y.

points: Add compost/manure/humus
Add sand
Dig drainage channels
Plough/till to aerate
Add lime to break up clay (flocculation)

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Name the layers labelled W and Z.

points: W - topsoil (1)
Z - bedrock/parent rock (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain the role of nitrogen-fixing bacteria in soil fertility.

points: They convert nitrogen gas from the air into nitrogen compounds (ammonium/nitrates) (1)
which plants use to make proteins (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: State ONE way in which decomposers improve soil fertility.

points: They break down dead plants and animals (1) and release minerals/nutrients into the soil and form humus (1)

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: Two people, A and B, each drank a solution containing 75 g of glucose after fasting. Their blood glucose levels were measured for 3 hours. The results are shown in Figure 5.
parts.figure: Figure 5. Blood glucose after a glucose drink

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State the blood glucose level of Person A after 30 minutes and after 120 minutes.

points: 30 min: 7.5 mmol per litre (1)
120 min: 5.0 mmol per litre (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Which person is MOST likely to have diabetes? Give TWO reasons from the graph.

points: Person B (1)
B's fasting glucose level is higher (8 compared with 5) (1)
B's level rises higher and stays high, not returning to normal after 3 hours (1)

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Explain how the level of blood glucose returned to normal in Person A.

points: The rise in blood glucose was detected by the pancreas (1)
the pancreas released insulin into the blood (1)
insulin caused glucose to be taken up by cells/stored as glycogen in the liver, lowering blood glucose (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State TWO ways in which a person with Type 2 diabetes can help to control the condition.

points: Eat a balanced diet low in sugar and refined carbohydrates
Exercise regularly
Lose excess weight
Take prescribed medication
Monitor blood glucose

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State TWO long-term effects of uncontrolled diabetes.

points: Blindness/eye damage
Kidney failure
Nerve damage
Poor wound healing/amputation
Heart disease/stroke

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Distinguish between the way the nervous system and the endocrine system send messages.

points: The nervous system sends electrical impulses along neurones, which are fast and short-lived (1)
the endocrine system sends hormones in the blood, which act more slowly but last longer (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Name the hormone produced by the adrenal glands.

points: Adrenaline
