items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Make a large, labelled drawing of the flower shown in Figure 6. Label SIX parts.

points: Clean continuous lines, no shading (1)
Large drawing (1)
All main parts included in correct proportion (1)
Any six correct labels: petal, sepal, anther, filament, stigma, style, ovary, ovule, receptacle (2 marks for six, 1 mark for three to five)
Ruled label lines that do not cross (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Measure the height of your drawing and calculate its magnification. Show your working.

points: Magnification = height of drawing ÷ actual height, e.g. 120 mm ÷ 60 mm (1)
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for working; 1 mark for correct magnification with ×

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Write a suitable title for your drawing.

points: e.g. 'Longitudinal section (L.S.) of a flower'
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark (must name the specimen and the view)

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State the function of EACH of the following: stigma; ovary; petal.

points: Stigma - receives pollen (1)
Ovary - contains ovules / develops into the fruit (1)
Petal - attracts insects for pollination (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Describe what happens from the time a pollen grain lands on the stigma until fertilisation.

points: The pollen grain grows a pollen tube down through the style (1)
the tube enters the ovule through the micropyle (1)
the male nucleus fuses with the female nucleus (egg cell) to form a zygote (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State TWO differences between insect-pollinated and wind-pollinated flowers.

points: Insect: large bright petals; wind: small dull petals
Insect: scent and nectar; wind: none
Insect: sticky/spiky pollen; wind: light, smooth pollen in large amounts
Insect: stigma inside the flower; wind: feathery stigma hanging outside

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Suggest ONE advantage of cross-pollination to a plant species.

points: It brings together genetic material from two different plants (1)
increasing variation in the offspring (1)
so the species is more likely to adapt to changes such as new diseases or climate (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

parts.figure: Figure 7. Blood cells

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Name cells X, Y and Z.

points: X - red blood cell
Y - phagocyte
Z - lymphocyte

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain how cells Y and Z work together to protect the body from infection.

points: Y (phagocytes) engulf and digest pathogens (1)
Z (lymphocytes) produce antibodies specific to the antigens on the pathogen (1)
antibodies clump/mark pathogens, making it easier for phagocytes to destroy them; memory cells remain (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Compare the xylem and the phloem in terms of what they carry and the direction of movement.

points: Xylem carries water and mineral salts (1)
phloem carries dissolved food/sugars (1)
xylem transport is upwards only, from roots to leaves; phloem transport is up and down to all parts (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain why a ring of bark removed from a tree trunk (ringing) may eventually kill the tree.

points: The phloem is just under the bark and is removed (1)
so sugars made in the leaves cannot reach the roots, which starve and die (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Name the blood vessel which carries blood from the left ventricle to the body.

points: Aorta

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State TWO differences between arteries and veins.

points: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry blood to the heart
Arteries have thick muscular walls; veins have thin walls
Veins have valves; arteries do not (except at the heart)
Blood in arteries is at high pressure; in veins low pressure

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Explain why a person with blood group O is called a universal donor.

points: Group O red cells have no A or B antigens, so they are not agglutinated by the recipient's antibodies.
